claim: Research laboratories in low- and middle-income countries face systemic challenges in conducting research and public health surveillance.
source: Research laboratories in low- and middle-income countries, where the global burden of disease is highest, face systemic challenges in conducting research and public health surveillance.
evidence: This is the main thesis statement of the manuscript, supported by multiple examples and experiences described throughout the text.

claim: The global burden of disease is highest in low- and middle-income countries.
source: Research laboratories in low- and middle-income countries, where the global burden of disease is highest, face systemic challenges in conducting research and public health surveillance.
evidence: This is stated as established fact in the abstract.

claim: Paywalls, customs regulations and lack of local suppliers hinder the scientific community in low- and middle-income countries.
source: An international effort is needed to overcome the paywalls, customs regulations and lack of local suppliers that hinder the scientific community in these countries.
evidence: This claim is supported by specific examples provided throughout the manuscript, including difficulties obtaining primers, media, and accessing journals.

claim: Research laboratories form the backbone of public health surveillance systems.
source: Research laboratories form the backbone of public health surveillance systems.
evidence: This is stated as a foundational premise in the manuscript.

claim: In the last two decades, low- and middle-income countries have experienced an enormous increase in research funding with support from groups like the Wellcome Trust, the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, and the World Health Organization.
source: In the last two decades, with support from groups like the Wellcome Trust, the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF), and the World Health Organization (WHO), low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) have experienced an enormous increase in research funding.
evidence: This is stated as a factual observation about funding trends over the past 20 years.

claim: The systemic and daily hindrances to conducting research and obtaining laboratory supplies and equipment in LMICs have not improved proportionately to the increase in research funding.
source: However, the systemic and daily hindrances to conducting research and obtaining laboratory supplies and equipment have not improved proportionately.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' experiences and examples provided throughout the manuscript.

claim: According to the WHO, the scarcity of health technologies in LMICs was partly responsible for the slow progress towards achieving the Millennium Development Goals.
source: According to the WHO, the scarcity of health technologies in LMICs was partly responsible for the slow progress towards achieving the Millennium Development Goals, which aimed to reduce morbidity and mortality (World Health Organization, 2014).
evidence: This claim is directly attributed to WHO and supported by a citation.

claim: The Millennium Development Goals aimed to reduce morbidity and mortality.
source: According to the WHO, the scarcity of health technologies in LMICs was partly responsible for the slow progress towards achieving the Millennium Development Goals, which aimed to reduce morbidity and mortality (World Health Organization, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a factual description of the MDG objectives.

claim: The scarcity of health technologies in LMICs is tied to barriers that must be overcome to acquire basic laboratory supplies for research.
source: This, we believe, is firmly tied to the barriers that must be overcome to acquire even the most basic laboratory supplies for research.
evidence: This is an inference made by the authors connecting technology scarcity to supply barriers.

claim: For almost every research study conducted in Bangladesh, researchers face a multitude of barriers that are almost non-existent in high-income settings.
source: For almost every research study we conduct in Bangladesh, we face a multitude of barriers that are almost non-existent in high-income settings.
evidence: This is based on the authors' direct experience conducting research in Bangladesh.

claim: Three members of the research team spent several weeks strategizing on how to obtain Thayer Martin media and supplements necessary to grow meningitis-causing bacteria because domestic vendors had stopped supplying them.
source: Earlier this year, three members of our team spent several weeks strategizing on how to obtain Thayer Martin media and supplements necessary to grow meningitis-causing bacteria, because domestic vendors had stopped supplying them.
evidence: This is a specific example from the authors' direct experience.

claim: It took over five months to secure a long-term local supply of Thayer Martin media and start processing samples.
source: It took us over five months to secure a long-term local supply and start processing the samples.
evidence: This is a specific data point from the authors' experience.

claim: The research team had collected 1,600 specimens from children but were not able to process them due to lack of supplies.
source: This is not a sustainable solution, but we needed the supplies urgently – we had already collected 1,600 specimens from children but were not able to process them.
evidence: This is a specific example with quantitative data from the authors' research.

claim: For researchers working in the US or Europe, ordering primers generally takes no longer than three days for delivery.
source: For anyone working in the US or Europe, ordering primers is generally one of the easiest and fastest steps, normally taking no longer than three days for delivery.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison point based on knowledge of research practices in high-income countries.

claim: In Bangladesh, the time to obtain primers can be as long as six months.
source: Here, however, running a PCR means thinking far ahead; the time to obtain primers can be as long as six months.
evidence: This is based on the authors' direct experience in Bangladesh.

claim: There are no manufacturers of PCR primers within Bangladesh.
source: There are no manufacturers within Bangladesh and clearing lab reagents through customs is still difficult.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the manufacturing infrastructure in Bangladesh.

claim: Clearing lab reagents through customs in Bangladesh is difficult.
source: There are no manufacturers within Bangladesh and clearing lab reagents through customs is still difficult.
evidence: This is based on the authors' direct experience with customs procedures.

claim: Supply struggles translate to a long lag time, often months, between conceiving an idea and performing experiments in Bangladesh.
source: These struggles usually translate to a long lag time, often months, between conceiving an idea and performing the experiments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' experiences with supply delays.

claim: Long lag times between conceiving ideas and performing experiments translate into blunted motivation and often redundant ideas.
source: This, in turn, translates into blunted motivation and, often, redundant ideas.
evidence: This is an inference about the psychological and scientific consequences of delays.

claim: The research team designed novel primers to identify mutations in antibiotic-resistant genes in Salmonella Typhi.
source: For example, we recently designed novel primers to identify mutations in antibiotic-resistant genes in Salmonella Typhi.
evidence: This is a specific example from the authors' research.

claim: By the time the primers arrived and experiments were completed, another group had published similar findings on antibiotic-resistant genes in Salmonella Typhi.
source: By the time the primers arrived, and we finished performing the experiments, another group had published similar findings.
evidence: This is a specific example from the authors' experience.

claim: In a scientific world where replication is undervalued, being scooped was a big loss for the team in terms of resources and intellectual effort.
source: In a scientific world where replication is undervalued it was a big loss for our team, both in terms of resources and intellectual effort.
evidence: This combines a statement about scientific culture (replication being undervalued) with an assessment of impact.

claim: Incidents of being scooped due to supply delays are commonplace in most LMIC research settings.
source: Such incidents are commonplace in most LMIC research settings but are rarely discussed or effectively acted upon.
evidence: This is a generalization based on the authors' knowledge of LMIC research environments.

claim: Incidents of being scooped due to supply delays are rarely discussed or effectively acted upon in LMIC research settings.
source: Such incidents are commonplace in most LMIC research settings but are rarely discussed or effectively acted upon.
evidence: This is an observation about the discourse around research challenges in LMICs.

claim: The current structure of academic publishing keeps results away from researchers in LMICs while still requiring them to publish in these forums for credibility.
source: The current structure of academic publishing keeps results away from researchers in LMICs, while still requiring them to publish in these forums for credibility.
evidence: This is an inference about the paradoxical nature of academic publishing for LMIC researchers.

claim: Institutions in LMICs, specifically non-profit research organizations, cannot afford to provide their members with unlimited access to scientific journals.
source: Institutions in LMICs, specifically non-profit research organizations like ours, cannot afford to provide their members with unlimited access to scientific journals, making it impossible for these researchers to access much of the scholarly literature.
evidence: This is based on the authors' direct experience at their institution.

claim: The inability to afford journal access makes it impossible for researchers in LMIC non-profit organizations to access much of the scholarly literature.
source: Institutions in LMICs, specifically non-profit research organizations like ours, cannot afford to provide their members with unlimited access to scientific journals, making it impossible for these researchers to access much of the scholarly literature.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the lack of institutional subscriptions.

claim: During journal clubs, members often talk about abstracts of exciting papers they would have presented had they not hit the paywall.
source: During our journal clubs, members often talk about abstracts of exciting papers they would have presented had they not hit the paywall.
evidence: This is a specific observation from the authors' institutional experience.

claim: The research team completed a small project evaluating a novel tool for detecting typhoidal Salmonella in the environment.
source: Recently, we completed a small project evaluating a novel tool for detecting typhoidal Salmonella in the environment.
evidence: This is a description of a specific research project conducted by the authors.

claim: The objective of the Salmonella detection study was to develop a low-cost PCR-based surveillance method for LMICs that cannot afford to establish or sustain traditional blood culture-based community surveillance.
source: The overarching objective of this study was to develop a low-cost PCR-based surveillance method for LMICs that cannot afford to establish or sustain traditional blood culture-based community surveillance.
evidence: This is a statement of the research objective from the authors' study.

claim: The Salmonella detection study received no external funding.
source: The whole study, for which we received no external funding, cost $3,864 (excluding personnel costs).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the funding status of the study.

claim: The Salmonella detection study cost $3,864 excluding personnel costs.
source: The whole study, for which we received no external funding, cost $3,864 (excluding personnel costs).
evidence: This is specific financial data from the authors' study.

claim: The journal where the Salmonella detection manuscript was submitted estimated a cost of $1,625 for publication.
source: The journal where we submitted the manuscript estimated a cost of $1,625 for publication, with an additional $2,500 required to make it open access.
evidence: This is specific financial data from the authors' publication experience.

claim: The journal required an additional $2,500 to make the Salmonella detection manuscript open access.
source: The journal where we submitted the manuscript estimated a cost of $1,625 for publication, with an additional $2,500 required to make it open access.
evidence: This is specific financial data from the authors' publication experience.

claim: The findings in the Salmonella detection paper were specifically targeted to groups in the Global South without access to most of the literature.
source: Although the findings reported in the paper were specifically targeted to groups like ours in the Global South without access to most of the literature, we had no option but to renounce the cost-prohibitive open access option and, in turn, limit the potential benefits of our study.
evidence: This is a statement about the intended audience of the research.

claim: The authors had no option but to renounce the cost-prohibitive open access option, limiting the potential benefits of their study.
source: Although the findings reported in the paper were specifically targeted to groups like ours in the Global South without access to most of the literature, we had no option but to renounce the cost-prohibitive open access option and, in turn, limit the potential benefits of our study.
evidence: This is a description of the authors' decision and its consequences.

claim: By not choosing open access, the authors played into the role of keeping the scholarly poor trapped in the vicious cycle of colonial science culture.
source: We too played into the role of keeping the scholarly poor trapped in the vicious cycle of colonial science culture.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the implications of their publication decision.

claim: The growth of science globally is slowed down by barriers that prevent access to knowledge and research supplies.
source: It is unacceptable that the growth of science globally is slowed down by barriers that prevent access to knowledge and research supplies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the examples and arguments presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The obstacles to research in LMICs are multifaceted but not impossible to overcome.
source: The obstacles are multifaceted, but not impossible to overcome.
evidence: This is a statement of the authors' perspective on the solvability of the problems.

claim: The HINARI Access to Research Initiative by the WHO provides free or low-cost access to journals to researchers affiliated with non-profit organizations in LMICs.
source: Examples of current efforts to improve access to the literature include the HINARI Access to Research Initiative by the WHO, which provides free or low-cost access to journals to researchers affiliated with non-profit organizations in LMICs (Research4Life, 2018).
evidence: This is a factual statement about an existing program, supported by a citation.

claim: Access to HINARI is based on GNP.
source: However, access to HINARI is based on GNP, so it excludes countries like India, Brazil and Indonesia, and many other countries will lose their eligibility as their economies develop (The PLoS Medicine Editors, 2006).
evidence: This is a factual statement about HINARI's eligibility criteria, supported by a citation.

claim: HINARI excludes countries like India, Brazil and Indonesia based on GNP criteria.
source: However, access to HINARI is based on GNP, so it excludes countries like India, Brazil and Indonesia, and many other countries will lose their eligibility as their economies develop (The PLoS Medicine Editors, 2006).
evidence: This is a factual statement about which countries are excluded, supported by a citation.

claim: Many countries will lose their HINARI eligibility as their economies develop.
source: However, access to HINARI is based on GNP, so it excludes countries like India, Brazil and Indonesia, and many other countries will lose their eligibility as their economies develop (The PLoS Medicine Editors, 2006).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the GNP-based eligibility criteria, supported by a citation.

claim: A slight rise in GNP does not make research organizations in a country resource-rich overnight.
source: However, a slight rise in GNP does not make research organizations in the country resource-rich overnight.
evidence: This is a logical argument about the disconnect between national economic indicators and institutional resources.

claim: Global collaboration is needed to push for universal access to scientific literature.
source: To fundamentally tackle this issue, we need global collaboration to push for universal access.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' analysis of the problem.

claim: Several European countries and institutions have moved to cancel their subscription with some giant publishers due to their slow progress towards open access.
source: Recently, several European countries and institutions have moved to cancel their subscription with some of the giant publishers due to their slow progress towards open access (Schiermeier, 2018; Yeager, 2018).
evidence: This is a factual statement about recent actions by European institutions, supported by citations.

claim: Many LMICs do not individually have the platform to negotiate with publishers.
source: Many LMICs do not individually have the platform to negotiate with publishers; however, collectively we may be able to expedite changes and shape the future of academic access.
evidence: This is an assessment of the negotiating power of individual LMICs.

claim: Collectively, LMICs may be able to expedite changes and shape the future of academic access.
source: Many LMICs do not individually have the platform to negotiate with publishers; however, collectively we may be able to expedite changes and shape the future of academic access.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about the potential power of collective action.

claim: If countries like Sweden and Germany come together with LMICs, it could prove to be a powerful platform for negotiating with publishers.
source: Furthermore, if countries like Sweden and Germany come together with LMICs, it could prove to be a powerful platform.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal about international collaboration.

claim: Many funding agencies now require all funded research to be published as open-access with associated fees being directly paid by the donor.
source: Many funding agencies now require all funded research to be published as open-access with associated fees being directly paid by the donor.
evidence: This is a statement about current funding agency policies.

claim: Donors usually have specific priorities, and well-intentioned efforts by individual donors can have asymmetrical impacts.
source: However, it is important to not lose sight of the fact that donors usually have specific priorities, and well-intentioned efforts by individual donors can have asymmetrical impacts, making certain research topics and publications available, while contradictory findings may not be.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of donor-driven open access policies.

claim: Donor-driven open access can make certain research topics and publications available while contradictory findings may not be.
source: However, it is important to not lose sight of the fact that donors usually have specific priorities, and well-intentioned efforts by individual donors can have asymmetrical impacts, making certain research topics and publications available, while contradictory findings may not be.
evidence: This is an inference about potential bias in what research becomes openly accessible.

claim: One solution could include donors like the BMGF working with local vendors or other organizations to ensure timely delivery of supplies to their grantees.
source: One solution could include donors, like the BMGF, working with local vendors or other organizations to ensure timely delivery of supplies to their grantees.
evidence: This is a proposed solution based on the authors' analysis.

claim: The research team was able to achieve timely supply delivery while conducting the ANISA study in collaboration with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
source: This is not a fanciful idea – we were able to achieve this while conducting the ANISA (Aetiology of Neonatal Infections in South Asia) study in collaboration with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC; Hibberd and Qazi, 2016; Saha et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a specific example from the authors' research experience, supported by citations.

claim: ANISA performed cutting-edge diagnostic tests in five sites, including rural sites, in India, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
source: ANISA performed cutting-edge diagnostic tests in five sites, including rural sites, in India, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
evidence: This is a description of the ANISA study scope.

claim: With the help of local CDC offices, the same equipment and research supplies were delivered to all ANISA laboratories without delays or hassles.
source: It was with the help of local CDC offices in these countries, who formed strong relationships with the relevant governments, that the same equipment and research supplies were delivered to all the laboratories without delays or hassles.
evidence: This is a specific example from the authors' experience with the ANISA study.

claim: Local CDC offices formed strong relationships with relevant governments to facilitate supply delivery for ANISA.
source: It was with the help of local CDC offices in these countries, who formed strong relationships with the relevant governments, that the same equipment and research supplies were delivered to all the laboratories without delays or hassles.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the CDC facilitated supply delivery.

claim: Recent budget cuts mean that the CDC may discontinue its work in 39 of the 49 countries it currently operates in.
source: However, recent budget cuts mean that the CDC may discontinue its work in 39 of the 49 countries it currently operates in (McKay, 2018).
evidence: This is a factual statement about potential CDC program cuts, supported by a citation.

claim: The WHO has the largest role in global health, putting it in a crucial position to facilitate changes.
source: Regardless of the CDC's future in global health, the WHO has the largest role in the field by far, putting it in a crucial position to facilitate changes.
evidence: This is a statement about WHO's position in global health.

claim: The WHO runs Invasive Bacterial Vaccine Preventable Disease surveillance studies in 58 countries.
source: The WHO runs Invasive Bacterial Vaccine Preventable Disease (IB-VPD) surveillance studies in 58 countries, where they have already set up offices that can facilitate the delivery of relevant supplies to supported laboratories (Hasan et al., 2018); the current process, however, often moves at a glacial pace and is highly bureaucratic.
evidence: This is a factual statement about WHO programs, supported by a citation.

claim: The WHO has set up offices in IB-VPD surveillance countries that can facilitate the delivery of relevant supplies to supported laboratories.
source: The WHO runs Invasive Bacterial Vaccine Preventable Disease (IB-VPD) surveillance studies in 58 countries, where they have already set up offices that can facilitate the delivery of relevant supplies to supported laboratories (Hasan et al., 2018); the current process, however, often moves at a glacial pace and is highly bureaucratic.
evidence: This is a statement about WHO infrastructure, supported by a citation.

claim: The current WHO process for facilitating supply delivery often moves at a glacial pace and is highly bureaucratic.
source: The WHO runs Invasive Bacterial Vaccine Preventable Disease (IB-VPD) surveillance studies in 58 countries, where they have already set up offices that can facilitate the delivery of relevant supplies to supported laboratories (Hasan et al., 2018); the current process, however, often moves at a glacial pace and is highly bureaucratic.
evidence: This is a critical assessment based on the authors' experience with WHO processes.

claim: Donors could leverage the systems and relationships already established by the WHO to help research laboratories acquire supplies for their own projects.
source: Donors could leverage the systems and relationships already established by the WHO to help research laboratories acquire supplies for their own projects.
evidence: This is a proposed solution based on existing WHO infrastructure.

claim: The WHO can work with governments in LMICs to assemble reasonable customs regulations for biological research products.
source: More sustainably, the WHO can work with governments in LMICs to assemble reasonable customs regulations for biological research products.
evidence: This is a proposed solution for addressing customs barriers.

claim: Working with governments to improve customs regulations would require extensive and honest partnerships and collaborations between multiple stakeholders, including donors, governments, WHO employees and local vendors.
source: This would require extensive and honest partnerships and collaborations between multiple stakeholders, including donors, governments, WHO employees and local vendors, and thus extra effort beyond just monetary support in the form of research grants.
evidence: This is an inference about what would be required to implement the proposed solution.

claim: Improving customs regulations requires extra effort beyond just monetary support in the form of research grants.
source: This would require extensive and honest partnerships and collaborations between multiple stakeholders, including donors, governments, WHO employees and local vendors, and thus extra effort beyond just monetary support in the form of research grants.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of effort required.

claim: Improving customs regulations can go a long way towards improving the prospects of scientific research in LMICs.
source: The results, however, can go a long way towards improving the prospects of scientific research in LMICs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the proposed solution.

claim: Without immediate and sustained interventions, the gap in resources between high-resource settings and low-resource settings will only worsen.
source: Without immediate and sustained interventions, the gap in resources between high-resource settings and low-resource settings will only worsen, jeopardizing research in LMICs further.
evidence: This is a prediction about future trends if no action is taken.

claim: Without immediate and sustained interventions, research in LMICs will be further jeopardized.
source: Without immediate and sustained interventions, the gap in resources between high-resource settings and low-resource settings will only worsen, jeopardizing research in LMICs further.
evidence: This is a prediction about the consequences of inaction.

claim: By uniting as one worldwide scientific community, appropriate steps can be taken to bring the scholarly poor out of literary poverty and make global health research truly global.
source: By uniting as one worldwide scientific community we can take appropriate steps to bring the scholarly poor out of literary poverty and make global health research truly global.
evidence: This is a call to action and speculative statement about what could be achieved through collective effort.
